analysis.one_liner: Adds sexual orientation and gender identity to federal civil rights protections in work, housing, credit, and public places.
analysis.headline: Introduced in April 2025 with 46 of 47 Senate Democrats and Independents as cosponsors, the bill has sat in the Judiciary Committee with no hearing, markup, or vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The Equality Act writes sexual orientation and gender identity into the core federal civil rights laws, so discrimination against LGBTQ people is treated the same as discrimination based on race or sex. It would apply in employment, housing, credit, jury service, federally funded programs, and public accommodations — and it expands 'public accommodations' beyond physical stores to include online retailers, health care providers, shelters, and transportation services. It also states that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act cannot be used as a defense to a claim under these civil rights laws.
analysis.who_benefits: LGBTQ people and women who face discrimination when applying for jobs, renting or buying housing, getting credit, seeking services at stores, shelters, or health care facilities, serving on juries, or participating in federally funded programs. The bill's findings point to evidence such as same-sex couples facing worse treatment in rental and elder housing, transgender people having about half the homeownership rate of non-transgender people, and LGBTQ youth being overrepresented in foster care. Children in the foster system would also benefit from a larger pool of willing foster and adoptive homes.
analysis.who_benefits_short: LGBTQ people and women facing discrimination

how_it_helps.text: Adds 'sex (including sexual orientation and gender identity)' to Title II public accommodations, Title VII employment, the Fair Housing Act, the Equal Credit Opportunity Act, federally funded programs, public education, and jury selection provisions of federal law.

Codifies the Supreme Court's Bostock decision by making explicit that existing sex discrimination bans cover sexual orientation and gender identity, instead of leaving the protection dependent on court interpretation.

Expands 'public accommodations' beyond physical places to include online retailers and service providers, health care, banks, shelters, transportation services, and individual providers of goods and services.
Bars the Religious Freedom Restoration Act from being used as a claim or defense against these civil rights provisions, closing an exemption critics said let discrimination continue.
Requires that individuals be allowed access to shared facilities such as restrooms and locker rooms consistent with their gender identity.

analysis.who_pays: Businesses and service providers would take on new compliance obligations and litigation exposure, including small and individual providers newly covered as public accommodations and online retailers. Faith-based child welfare agencies and other religious organizations would lose the ability to decline service to same-sex couples or LGBTQ individuals while operating under these laws, and all defendants would lose the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a defense in these cases.

drawbacks.text: The bill states that the Religious Freedom Restoration Act 'shall not provide a claim concerning, or a defense to a claim under' any covered civil rights title, eliminating the main statutory shield religious organizations have used against these mandates.

It requires access to shared facilities — restrooms, locker rooms, dressing rooms — in accordance with gender identity, the provision that has drawn the strongest objection from critics concerned about sex-separated spaces.
It broadens public accommodations law to reach individual providers and online businesses, not just physical establishments, which expands the range of businesses exposed to discrimination claims.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and targeted: federal law now protects LGBTQ people in employment (after Bostock) but only patchily in housing, credit, and public services, and this bill would close those gaps with the same enforcement machinery used for race discrimination. The costs fall on businesses facing new legal obligations and on religious providers who would lose exemptions they currently hold, and the removal of the Religious Freedom Restoration Act defense is a genuine, deliberate trade-off that supporters should own. How heavily to weigh that trade-off is the core of the dispute, and the bill makes no attempt to accommodate it.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and referred to the Judiciary Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Senator Merkley introduced the Equality Act in the Senate on April 29, 2025.
It was read twice and referred to the Committee on the Judiciary the same day, and no further action appears in the record.
46 senators — 44 of 45 Senate Democrats and both Senate Independents — signed on as cosponsors; no Republican did.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost anything from the bill itself: it has not moved, so current law — which protects against employment discrimination after Bostock but leaves housing, credit, and public-accommodations gaps — remains in place. Businesses and religious organizations retain their current exemptions, and LGBTQ people remain without the explicit protections the bill would provide.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo holds; no one has moved yet

for.name: Sen. Jeff Merkley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Equality Act in the Senate and recruited a nearly full slate of Democratic and Independent cosponsors.

for.name: 44 of 45 Senate Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill, including the party leader, leaving only one Democratic senator off the bill.

against.name: Senate Republicans
against.what_they_did: No Republican senator cosponsored the bill, leaving it without the support needed to advance.

against.name: Sen. Chuck Grassley
against.what_they_did: Has not scheduled the bill for a committee hearing or markup; it has sat in his committee since referral.

sides.party_line_note: Support is nearly unanimous among Senate Democrats and Independents — 46 of 47 — and entirely absent among Republicans, with no Republican cosponsor.

industries.industry: Faith-based child welfare and adoption agencies
industries.note: Agencies that refuse to serve same-sex couples or LGBTQ individuals would have to comply or forgo federal funding, since the bill adds sexual orientation and gender identity to the nondiscrimination rules for federally funded programs. The bill's own findings argue this would enlarge the pool of homes for children waiting in foster care.

The bill bars the Religious Freedom Restoration Act as a claim or defense under the covered civil rights titles, removing the main legal shield these organizations have used to decline service on religious grounds.

industries.industry: Employers and retail/service businesses (including online retailers)
industries.note: Large employers already face the Bostock rule in employment, but the bill extends coverage to housing, credit, and a much broader definition of public accommodations that includes online providers and individual service businesses, creating new compliance and litigation exposure. For businesses serving consumers, the bill describes this as creating a level playing field and a larger customer base.

analysis.trajectory: With Republicans holding 55 Senate seats and no Republican cosponsor, the bill is very unlikely to get a committee markup or floor vote this Congress. Its House counterpart passed in earlier, differently-composed Congresses but never became law, and this Congress's math makes that path harder still; barring a major political shift, expect it to die in committee when this Congress ends in January 2027.
